_source: Paraphrased from the DBE 'Mathematics Teaching and Learning Framework for South Africa: Teaching Mathematics for Understanding' (draft 6, print date 27 Sep 2018), with page numbers as printed. Entries marked 'Katlego team' are our own and need teacher review. Short paraphrases only; nothing is quoted to learners.

methods: Balance: do the same to both sides until x is alone
Undo in reverse order: last thing done to x is undone first
Bar model: draw the parts and take away the known part
Guess, check and improve: try a number, see if it works, adjust
misconceptions: Doing an operation to one side only

entries.source: DBE TMU framework, Senior Phase, pp. 54-57
methods: Eliminate by inspection: the sign of m against the slope, equal intercepts only when m = 1
Read c as the y-intercept, then substitute another point to find m
Gradient formula with any two points on the line
Rise over run on the grid, from any point to any point on the line
misconceptions: Reading the x- and y-intercepts straight into m and c

entries.source: DBE TMU framework, Senior Phase, pp. 50-53
methods: Draw the rectangle around the triangle: the triangle is half the rectangle
Check with numbers on a grid: two smaller rectangles, half of each
misconceptions: Area always means length x breadth
Using a slanted side as the height

entries.source: DBE TMU framework, Senior Phase, pp. 53-54
methods: Check both conditions first: multiplying AND the same base, then add exponents
Write the powers out as repeated multiplication to see why the law works
Sort cases where the law applies, where like terms add instead, and where nothing simplifies
misconceptions: Adding exponents when the powers are added, not multiplied

entries.source: DBE TMU framework, Senior Phase, pp. 57-58
methods: Start from the two rows that differ by one shape and compare them
Assume a value, then test it against another row or column; drop it if it fails
misconceptions: Two different shapes given the same number

entries.source: DBE TMU framework, Senior Phase, pp. 58-61
methods: Check every part of the definition: exactly two angles AND they add up to 180 degrees
Find a counterexample: two angles that add to 180 but are not next to each other
misconceptions: Three angles on a line can be supplementary

methods: Area model: an x by x square plus two strips of (b/2)x; the missing corner is (b/2)^2
Procedure: halve the x-coefficient, square it, add it (and subtract it in an expression)
misconceptions: Adding (b/2)^2 to one side of an equation only

methods: Find two factors of the constant that add to the x-coefficient, split the middle term, take out common factors
Multiply back with the distributive law to check
misconceptions: Choosing factors that multiply correctly but add to the wrong sign

methods: Trial and error: draw a few rectangles with the same perimeter
Table of values for length, width and area
Graph area against length and read the turning point
Complete the square: A(x) = a(x - p)^2 + q, the maximum is q
Axis of symmetry: x = -b/2a, then substitute
Calculus (Grade 12): set A'(x) = 0
misconceptions: A square is not a rectangle

methods: Rewrite in exponential form: log_b(x) = y means b^y = x
Table of powers of the base: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...
Real context: how many times must you double (or fold paper) to reach the number?

entries.source: DBE TMU framework, FET, pp. 65-66 and 74-75
methods: Reasoning chain: each step A => B => C names the theorem that justifies it
Measure a few cases first (or drag points in GeoGebra), then prove the conjecture
misconceptions: Using what the diagram looks like instead of a theorem
